newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Does Wisconsin convention center have Wright stuff?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Does Wisconsin convention center have Wright stuff?.

text.p: Nearly 60 years ago, Frank Lloyd Wright first sketched his dream of a civic centre jutting out over Lake Monona.

The doors of the building he designed are finally about to open as a convention centre, with thousands expected to attend festivities this weekend that will include light shows, public tours and private parties. But just as controversy dogged Wright's modernistic designs from the leaky-roofed Johnson Wax building in nearby Racine (1939) to the sloping galleries of the Guggenheim Museum in New York (1959), Monona Terrace has set off grumbling as well as praise.

"This building would be inconceivable without Frank Lloyd Wright," said Tony Puttnam, the 62-year-old former Wright student who became "the architect of record" on the project. "He knew (Monona Terrace) wasn't going to be built while he was alive, but he said, 'Someday, it will be.' It is wonderful for me to see a good idea have its day," Puttnam told Reuters.

The 130,000 square-foot (12,000 square metre) steel-and-concrete building -- distinguished by cylinders, spirals and arches -- has changed Madison's skyline, even though it is only a few stories high. The buff-coloured structure juts out 90 feet (27 metres) from the lake's shoreline, providing a visual pedestal for the grand state Capitol rotunda behind it.

Wright designed Monona Terrace during a fertile period in his career when he also completed the Johnson Wax administration building. Earlier, he founded the famed "prairie school" of architecture sprung from his native Midwest's flat, horizontal landscape and evolved the concept of "organic" architecture fluent with the natural environment.
WEDDING CAKE OR BALL-AND-CHAIN
Some compare Monona Terrace to a wedding cake, others see a necklace, still others feel it is a ball-and-chain of debt.
"This building is like an ornament the city wears around its neck," said Jim Dennis, an art history professor at the University of Wisconsin who lives in a Wright-designed house.

While the sweeping beauty of the $67 million centre quieted some opponents, critics are still rehashing the debate that has long outlived Wright, who died in 1959. One bone of contention centres on what Wright would have thought about the final product. The weekly Isthmus newspaper concluded in a piece entitled "Wright and Wrong" that the architect would have been ambivalent.

Critic Jody Clowes said Wright's design, envisioning government offices and an auditorium, was impractical as a modern-day convention centre. Without dramatic changes, Monona Terrace would have been a museum piece, she wrote.

"So, since we are unwilling to give up on the master's design but equally unwilling to actually follow his difficult precepts, we have this hybrid beast instead, its radically reconceived interior shoehorned into a lovingly archived facade," Clowes wrote.

"The lake views are tremendous. The facade is wonderful, and clearly retains the mark of Wright's genius. But this revised structure represents a compromise of the very essence of Wright's architecture: its design integrity. The promise of this long-awaited building has not been achieved."
'MISTAKE ON THE LAKE'

More biting criticism is being circulated in a slick brochure entitled "Mistake on the Lake" from a group that calls itself "Citizens Against Public Idiocy." The brochure, with a revised logo of "Frank Lloyd Wrong," parodies the grand opening advertisements: "Share the dream gone sour; Blantant elitism; Pretentiousness; Condescension; Your tax dollars; Leaky roof?; No boats; and no restaurants."
Nobody said building the centre would be easy.

"I doubt that any of the folks who have been hostile to this project, or dubious about the merits of Frank Lloyd Wright and his work, will instantly change their minds when they walk into the building for the first time," William Cronon, a University of Wisconsin history professor, said. "But the view is stunning and I suspect they'll have to be at least a little bit moved almost in spite of themselves."

Controversy always followed the flamboyant, egotistical Wright, a one-time engineering student here, but the decades of delays and debate surrounding Monona Terrace surprised even Madison, where no building seems to go up without a fuss.

Even if the opening goes smoothly, the debate will continue. City officials were still figuring out how much of a public subsidy should be appropriated to build a needed hotel nearby. The subsidy could be as much as $20 million.
And many are still griping that the convention centre will operate at a deficit for many years. The Isthmus estimated the average Madison homeowner will shell out $1,000 over 20 years.

But there also appear to be many supporters, including those who bought more than 8,000 individually inscribed tiles that cover the building's expansive roof. Among buyers who paid between $95 and $1,200 per tile were Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson, scout troops, school classes and President Bill Clinton's Health & Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala.
Shalala, the local university's former chancellor, had her tile inscribed for a beloved pet: "Bucky the dog."
